title: India Becomes Third Country With Private Orbital Launch as Skyroot's Vikram-1 Makes History
excerpt: Hyderabad-based Skyroot Aerospace's maiden orbital launch from Sriharikota puts India alongside the US and China in an exclusive club, just six years after the country opened its space sector to private enterprise.
body:
• Skyroot Aerospace successfully launched Vikram-1, India's first privately built orbital rocket, from Sriharikota on July 18, making India the third country after the US and China to achieve a private orbital launch.
  • Skyroot became India's first space-tech unicorn after raising $60 million at a $1.1 billion valuation, with investors including Sherpalo Ventures and GIC.
  • India now has nearly 400 space startups and an $8.4 billion space economy, just six years after opening the sector to private players in 2020.
  • Vikram-1 carried four satellites into a 450-km orbit, including payloads from Indian startups Grahaa and Cosmoserve and German startup Dcubed.

Mission Aagaman: The Arrival

At 12:05 p.m. local time on July 18, a seven-story rocket built by a company founded by two former ISRO engineers lifted off from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. Fifteen minutes later, Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 reached a 450-kilometer orbit, and India entered an exclusive club.

https://x.com/firstpost/status/2083893075513143681

The mission, named "Aagaman" — Hindi for "The Arrival" — marked the first orbital launch by a private company in India. With it, the country became only the third in the world where a domestic private firm has reached orbit, after the United States and China. Skyroot also became the first company globally to achieve orbit on its maiden launch attempt.

"What the world witnessed today is the result of years of work by our team, our partners, and suppliers across the country. It proves that India has the talent, the technology, and the industrial strength to build launch vehicles that meet the world's standards."

— Pawan Kumar Chandana, CEO and co-founder, Skyroot Aerospace

Prime Minister Narendra Modi called it "a defining moment in India's space journey," adding that the growing participation of the private sector was "opening new frontiers and accelerating innovation."

From ISRO Engineers to Unicorn Founders

Skyroot was founded in 2018 by Pawan Kumar Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka, both former scientists at the Indian Space Research Organisation. The company's first milestone came in November 2022 when it launched Vikram-S, a suborbital test rocket — the first privately built rocket to reach space from India.

Vikram-1 is a different proposition entirely. The 22-meter-tall rocket is a full commercial launch vehicle capable of carrying 350 kilograms into low Earth orbit. It features three solid fuel stages plus a final liquid stage powered by a 3D-printed engine that can start, stop, and restart in space to place payloads in precise orbits. The airframe is built primarily from carbon-composite materials rather than metals, significantly reducing weight.

Ahead of the launch, Skyroot raised $60 million in a funding round that valued the company at $1.1 billion — making it India's first space-tech unicorn. The round was co-led by Sherpalo Ventures, founded by Alphabet board member Ram Shriram, and Singapore sovereign wealth fund GIC, with additional debt managed by BlackRock-affiliated funds.

The Broader Ecosystem

Skyroot's success is the most visible result of a policy revolution that began in 2020. Before that year, building and launching rockets and satellites was the exclusive domain of ISRO. The government's decision to open the sector to private enterprise, creating the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) as a regulatory framework, unleashed a wave of startup activity.

India now has nearly 400 space startups, and the government estimates the country's space economy is worth $8.4 billion. Skyroot leaned heavily on ISRO's infrastructure in the buildup to the launch, with the agency lending its facilities and expertise for testing, fueling, and launch operations — a model that analysts compare to the early relationship between NASA and SpaceX in the United States.

"That state-enables-private-executes model is exactly what worked in America," wrote Torsten Kriening, CEO of SpaceWatch.Global, in an analysis for IEEE Spectrum.

Commercial Ambitions and Competition

The Vikram-1 launch was more than a technology demonstration. The rocket successfully delivered four commercial payloads into orbit: a satellite from Skyroot itself, two from Indian startups Grahaa Space and Cosmoserve — the latter a robotic arm designed for orbital debris removal — and a technology demonstration payload from German startup Dcubed.

Skyroot has said Vikram-1 could begin regular commercial operations as early as next year, with its Hyderabad factory capable of building one rocket per month. The company is also developing Vikram-2, a more powerful rocket with a cryogenic engine capable of carrying 900 kg to low Earth orbit, with a first flight planned for 2027.

Several competitors are close behind. Chennai-based Agnikul Cosmos and Bengaluru-based Astrobase Space Technologies and EtherealX are all developing their own launch vehicles. Whether the Indian market can sustain multiple private launch companies remains an open question, particularly with SpaceX's Transporter rideshare missions driving down costs.

"The graveyard of small launchers is full of companies that flew once and stumbled on flights two, three, and four. That is where failures statistically live."

— Torsten Kriening, CEO, SpaceWatch.Global

What It Means for Indian Engineers Abroad

For the thousands of Indian aerospace engineers working at companies like SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Boeing in the United States and Europe, Skyroot's success opens a different question: whether India's private space sector is now mature enough to build serious careers at home. Skyroot employs over 1,000 people, and the broader ecosystem's demand for talent is accelerating.

India's space ambitions now extend well beyond ISRO's government missions. The private sector is building the rockets, the satellites, and — for the first time — the commercial pathways to orbit.
